posts.title: MCP is the integration layer nobody asked for but everyone needs
posts.hook: I stopped writing API wrappers three months ago.
posts.body:
I stopped writing API wrappers three months ago.

Model Context Protocol changed how I connect tools to agents. Instead of writing bespoke integration code for every new data source, I define a server once and every agent in my stack can use it.

Attio CRM, Apollo enrichment, Google Drive, Typefully for publishing. All MCP servers. All available to any Claude Code session without importing a single library.

The before:
- Write a Python wrapper for Apollo
- Write another for Attio
- Maintain auth logic in both
- Debug serialization edge cases forever

The after:
- Point the agent at the MCP server
- It discovers the tools itself
- It calls them with the right params
- I go do something else

The real unlock isn't "AI can call APIs." That's been possible. The unlock is that adding a new data source to your entire agent fleet takes 20 minutes instead of a week.

I run about 15 MCP servers now. Some are official connectors, some are custom scripts I wrapped in the protocol. The agents don't care which is which. They just see tools.

If you're still hand-wiring every integration into every agent... you're solving a problem that's already been solved.

remixes.label: before-after-workflow
remixes.hook: Adding a new tool to my agent stack used to take a full day. Now it takes 11 minutes.
remixes.body:
Adding a new tool to my agent stack used to take a full day. Now it takes 11 minutes.

The old workflow: read the API docs. Write an auth wrapper. Handle pagination. Parse the response into something my agent understands. Write tests. Deploy. Repeat for the next tool.

The MCP workflow: define a server with the endpoints I need. Point any agent at it. Done.

I currently run MCP servers for my CRM, email enrichment, file storage, and social publishing. Every one of them is accessible to every Claude Code session on my machine. No imports. No dependency management. No version conflicts between tools.

The part nobody talks about: MCP isn't just about saving time on the initial integration. It's about what happens when you swap tools. When I moved from one CRM to another, I updated one server definition. Every agent that touched CRM data kept working. Zero refactoring downstream.

The real unlock is composability. My agents don't know or care which specific tools they're talking to. They just know "CRM" and "enrichment" and "publishing." The MCP layer handles the rest.

This is what an actual integration layer looks like. Not Zapier. Not iPaaS. A protocol that treats tools as interchangeable capabilities.

remixes.hook: I dismissed MCP as hype for two months. Then I counted my API wrapper files.
remixes.body:
I dismissed MCP as hype for two months. Then I counted my API wrapper files.

47 files. Across 9 projects. Most of them doing the same thing: authenticate, fetch, transform, return. Half of them broken because an API changed and I hadn't noticed yet.

My skepticism was simple: why do I need a protocol when REST works fine? The answer isn't that REST doesn't work. It's that writing the same glue code 47 times doesn't work.

MCP flipped the model. Instead of every agent knowing how to talk to every tool, each tool exposes itself once. The agent just asks for what it needs.

Practical example: I wanted my content pipeline to pull analytics from Typefully, cross-reference with CRM data from Attio, and enrich contacts through Apollo. Old world, that's three custom integrations, three auth flows, three data transformation layers. MCP world, I pointed my agent at three servers and described what I wanted in plain English.

The protocol itself is simple. JSON-RPC over stdio or HTTP. The magic isn't in the spec. It's in the fact that every new tool I add makes every existing agent more capable without touching a line of agent code.

I went from skeptic to running 6 MCP servers in production in about three weeks.

posts.title: 14 tools that don't talk to each other
posts.hook: Your GTM stack isn't a stack. It's a junk drawer.
posts.body:
Your GTM stack isn't a stack. It's a junk drawer.

14 tools. 14 logins. 14 billing cycles. And the data lives in none of them correctly.

I spent two years in RevOps stitching together Salesforce, Outreach, ZoomInfo, 6sense, Gong, and whatever else the team bought at a conference. The integration budget alone was six figures. The data still didn't match.

So I stopped stitching.

Now I build the core GTM engine in SQLite + Python + Claude Code. Enrichment runs through Apollo and Exa APIs directly. Sequencing goes through a programmable sender I control. CRM is Attio with MCP access so the agent can read and write without me touching the UI.

Total monthly cost for the infrastructure: under $500.

The 14-tool stack wasn't solving a technology problem. It was solving a "nobody here can code" problem. And that problem just got mass-disrupted by coding agents.

You don't need a platform that "integrates with 200+ tools." You need one agent that can call 5 APIs and a database that you own.

The consolidation wave in GTM isn't coming from better platforms. It's coming from founders who realize they can just... build it.

remixes.body:
I audited a client's GTM stack last month. They were spending $214,000 a year on tools that shared zero data.

Salesforce. Outreach. ZoomInfo. 6sense. Gong. Drift. Clearbit. Marketo. LeanData. And five more I'd never heard of.

Each tool had its own version of the truth. The contact count in the CRM didn't match enrichment. The engagement data in the sequencer didn't match the intent platform. Marketing's lead count and sales' lead count were different numbers describing different things.

The integration budget was $87,000 annually. Consultants, middleware, custom Apex code, a part-time contractor maintaining Marketo webhooks. And the data still didn't match.

So here's what I actually recommend now: pick three tools maximum. A database you control, an enrichment source, and a sending mechanism. Write the connective tissue yourself. It's less code than you think, especially with agents doing the transformation work.

The GTM stack of 2025 wasn't a technology problem. It was a purchasing problem. Every team bought their own solution. Nobody owned the data model. The "stack" was just a pile.

The uncomfortable math: most companies would get better results from a $500/month setup they actually understand than a $200k/year constellation nobody can debug.

remixes.label: founder-first-person
remixes.hook: I used to think more tools meant more capability. Then I became the person who had to make them work together.
remixes.body:
I used to think more tools meant more capability. Then I became the person who had to make them work together.

In my RevOps days, every quarter started the same way. Sales wanted a new sequencer. Marketing wanted a new intent platform. CS wanted a new health scoring tool. And I was the one who had to make the data flow between all of them.

The dirty secret of the modern GTM stack: the tools work fine individually. It's the connections that break everything.

A contact gets enriched in ZoomInfo but the field mapping to Salesforce truncates the job title. An intent signal fires in 6sense but the routing rule in LeanData doesn't match because someone changed a picklist value. A Gong call gets logged but the activity sync to Outreach is 6 hours behind.

You don't have a tool problem. You have 14 tools that were never designed to share a data model.

What I do now is different. I own the data layer. A single database where every record has one canonical shape. Tools plug into that layer. They don't define it.

The result: fewer tools, cleaner data, faster execution. And I can actually debug problems because I understand every connection in the system.

The best GTM stack is the one you can explain on a whiteboard in under two minutes.

posts.title: Cold outbound isn't dead, your research is
posts.hook: I sent 12 cold emails last week. Got 5 replies.
posts.body:
I sent 12 cold emails last week. Got 5 replies.

Not 12,000. Twelve.

The lazy outbound era trained us to think in volume. Blast 5,000 contacts, get a 2% reply rate, call it a win. But 2% of garbage is still garbage.

The shift I made: spend 80% of the time on research, 20% on writing.

For each of those 12 emails, I had:
- Their recent Reddit activity scraped and summarized
- Job postings from the last 30 days analyzed for pain signals
- Tech stack changes from BuiltWith diffs
- A specific hypothesis about what problem they're solving right now

All of that research was automated. Claude Code pulls the signals, scores relevance, writes a brief. I review the brief, write the email in 3 minutes.

The people replying aren't replying because the email was clever. They're replying because I clearly did the work. In a world flooded with AI-generated spray-and-pray, showing that you actually understand someone's situation is the differentiation.

Volume is the old game. Signal density is the new one.

remixes.hook: The email that got me a meeting with a VP at a Series C company was 4 sentences long. The research behind it took 45 minutes.
remixes.body:
The email that got me a meeting with a VP at a Series C company was 4 sentences long. The research behind it took 45 minutes.

Here's exactly what those 45 minutes looked like.

Minutes 1 to 10: Reddit and community scanning. I found two comments from this person in a niche subreddit about their specific pain point. Not generic industry stuff. Their actual words about a real problem.

Minutes 10 to 25: Job posting analysis. Their company had three open roles that told me exactly what they were building. The required skills in those postings revealed technology decisions. The seniority levels revealed budget priorities.

Minutes 25 to 35: Company context. Recent funding, tech stack signals from BuiltWith, any public content from their team. I found a podcast episode where their CTO mentioned a specific workflow bottleneck.

Minutes 35 to 45: Writing the email. Four sentences. Referenced the Reddit comment. Connected it to the job posting pattern. Proposed a specific, narrow solution to the bottleneck their CTO mentioned publicly.

The reply came in 3 hours.

This doesn't scale to 5,000 emails. It's not supposed to. It scales to 12 emails a week that actually start conversations. I'll take 5 replies from 12 sends over 100 replies from 5,000 sends every single time. The math works better and the conversations are better.

remixes.body:
The highest-performing outbound rep I know sends fewer than 20 emails a week.

That sentence should bother you if you're running an SDR team measured on activity volume.

The outbound industry spent the last five years optimizing for the wrong metric. Send volume. Sequences per rep. Emails per day. The entire infrastructure, the sending tools, the warmup services, the inbox rotation, all of it was built to help you send more. Not send better.

Here's what happens when you flip the ratio. Instead of 20% research and 80% sending, go 80% research and 20% sending.

You learn things that change the email entirely. A prospect's Reddit comment reveals what they actually care about, not what their LinkedIn headline says. Their company's job postings reveal what they're building next quarter. A podcast appearance reveals the specific language they use to describe their problems.

Armed with that, your email doesn't sound like outbound. It sounds like someone who's been paying attention.

I sent 12 emails last week. Got 5 replies. That's a 42% reply rate. The math doesn't come from a clever subject line or a fancy sending tool. It comes from knowing enough about the person to say something they actually want to respond to.

Volume outbound is a tax on your brand. Every bad email makes the next good one harder to land.

posts.title: The hybrid inference stack
posts.hook: Not every agent task deserves Opus pricing.
posts.body:
Not every agent task deserves Opus pricing.

I run a three-tier inference stack:

1. Haiku for classification, routing, and simple extraction. Costs almost nothing. Runs thousands of times a day in my content pipeline.

2. Sonnet for drafting, summarization, and mid-complexity analysis. My daily cron jobs, Reddit scouting, and enrichment scoring all run here.

3. Opus for architecture decisions, complex content creation, and anything that touches production code. This is where I sit in Claude Code right now.

The mistake I see teams make: they default everything to the most expensive model because "it's the best." Then they get the bill and shut down the whole project.

My enrichment pipeline processes ~2,000 contacts per run. If I ran that through Opus, it would cost more than the tool subscriptions I replaced. Through Haiku with a Sonnet fallback for ambiguous cases, it costs less than a coffee.

The art isn't picking the best model. It's knowing which task needs which tier.

Routing logic doesn't need to be fancy either. A simple confidence threshold on the cheaper model, escalate to the next tier when it's unsure. Three if-statements, not a framework.
posts.cta: Where are you overusing expensive models for tasks that don't need them?

inspired_by.author: Marcus Holloway
inspired_by.summary: We just cut our agent inference costs 61% by moving from API calls to self-hosted Llama 3.1 for the retrieval layer, keeping frontier models only for final synthesis. Most teams are massively over-spending on the wrong part of the stack. Here's the architecture decision tree we use.

remixes.label: cost-disaster-story
remixes.hook: I burned $400 in API costs in one afternoon because I routed everything through the same model.
remixes.body:
I burned $400 in API costs in one afternoon because I routed everything through the same model.

I was running a content pipeline that classified Reddit posts, scored relevance, drafted responses, and summarized findings. Every step used the same model. The big one. Because it was easy and the outputs were good.

Then I checked the usage dashboard.

80% of those API calls were classification tasks. Binary decisions. "Is this post relevant? Yes or no." I was paying premium pricing for a model to answer questions a much smaller, cheaper model handles perfectly.

That afternoon taught me the tiered inference pattern I use now.

Tier 1, the smallest model: classification, routing, extraction, formatting. Tasks where the answer space is narrow and the reasoning is shallow. This handles about 70% of my total API calls at roughly 1/30th the cost per call.

remixes.hook: Model routing is the most underrated architecture decision in AI-native products.
remixes.body:
Model routing is the most underrated architecture decision in AI-native products.

Most teams pick one model and use it everywhere. It's the path of least resistance. One API key, one set of prompts, one billing line item. Simple.

But simple and smart aren't the same thing.

Think about how you'd staff a team. You wouldn't assign your most senior engineer to rename variables. You wouldn't have an intern architect your database. You match capability to complexity.

The same logic applies to inference. A classification task and a complex writing task don't need the same model. Sending both to the flagship is like having your senior engineer rename variables. It works, but it's wasteful.

My routing logic is straightforward. If the task has a constrained output space (yes/no, category labels, structured extraction), it goes to the smallest model. If it requires synthesis across multiple inputs or creative generation, it goes to mid-tier. If it involves architecture, strategy, or any task where a wrong answer cascades into more wrong answers, it goes to the flagship.

The implementation is simple. A router function at the entry point of each pipeline that checks the task type and calls the appropriate model. Maybe 20 lines of code total. The cost savings compound daily.

The bonus: this forces you to actually categorize your AI tasks by complexity, which makes your entire system easier to reason about.

posts.title: Building in public is the marketing channel
posts.hook: My best-performing LinkedIn posts aren't about marketing. They're screenshots of my terminal.
posts.body:
My best-performing LinkedIn posts aren't about marketing. They're screenshots of my terminal.

No graphic designer. No content calendar committee. No three rounds of review. Just "here's what I built today, here's how it works, here's the code."

The pattern I've noticed over 6 months of posting build logs:

- Tactical posts with real implementation details get 3-5x the engagement of opinion posts
- Screenshots of actual output outperform polished graphics
- Posts that admit something broke get more comments than posts about wins
- The audience self-selects. The people who engage with build logs are the people who actually build things. Those are the people I want to talk to.

I'm not anti-strategy. But the strategy is simple: show the work. Every day I'm in Claude Code building GTM infrastructure. That work IS the content. The newsletter, the LinkedIn posts, the Reddit threads... they're all just narrating what already happened.

The founders I see winning at content right now aren't hiring content teams. They're opening their laptop, building something, and writing about it before they close the lid.

The content strategy is the build strategy. They're the same thing.

I deleted my content calendar six months ago. My engagement tripled.

The calendar was killing my best content. I'd schedule "thought leadership" posts weeks in advance, and by the time they published, the moment had passed. The take was stale. The energy was flat.

What replaced it: I post what I build, when I build it.

Monday I shipped a new cron job that scouts Reddit for outbound signals. Took a screenshot of the terminal output and the scoring logic. Posted it with a quick explanation of how the scoring works. That post outperformed two weeks of planned content.

Wednesday I hit a weird bug in my MCP server configuration. Documented the fix in 4 paragraphs. Posted it. Three people DM'd me saying they hit the same issue.

The pattern is consistent: real work, documented in real time, beats polished content planned in advance. Every time.

Why? Because the energy is different. When you're posting about something you just did, the specificity is natural. You don't have to manufacture details. The frustration, the solution, the "oh that's why it works" moment. It's all there because you just lived it.

Content calendars optimize for consistency. Build logs optimize for resonance. I'll take resonance.

The best part: this approach takes less time. No brainstorming sessions. No drafts sitting in review. The work IS the content.

The raw stuff wins. Consistently. Not by a little. By 3 to 5x on engagement.

Here's my theory on why: the internet has a credibility crisis. Everyone has access to the same AI writing tools, the same design templates, the same carousel generators. Polished content no longer signals quality. It signals "this person knows how to use Canva."

The content format I use most: short text post describing what I built or fixed, a screenshot of it working, and one specific takeaway someone could apply today.

No graphic designer. No review committee. No polishing. Just proof of work.

I think we're entering an era where showing your work becomes the primary trust signal in professional content. The people who can demonstrate capability, not just describe it, will own their niches.

posts.title: RevOps identity crisis is actually an opportunity
posts.hook: RevOps teams are splitting into two camps and only one survives the agent era.
posts.body:
RevOps teams are splitting into two camps and only one survives the agent era.

Camp A: manually updating Salesforce fields, building reports in spreadsheets, chasing reps to log activities. Administrative RevOps.

Camp B: writing SQL against the warehouse, building enrichment pipelines, automating lead routing with code. Engineering RevOps.

Camp A gets automated first. An agent can update CRM fields, generate reports, and nag reps better than a human. That work disappears within 18 months.

Camp B becomes more valuable. Someone still needs to architect the data model, decide which signals matter, and build the logic that connects enrichment to routing to sequencing. Agents accelerate this work but can't replace the judgment.

The RevOps people I see thriving right now are the ones who learned Python or SQL in the last year. Not because they need to be engineers. Because they need to speak the language of the systems that are replacing their old workflow.

If your RevOps role is mostly clicking buttons in tools, start building the thing that clicks the buttons for you. That project is your job security and your next role's resume line.

The RevOps role you were hired for two years ago no longer exists.

Not because the company restructured. Because the work changed underneath you.

Two years ago, RevOps meant: configure Salesforce flows, build reports, maintain data hygiene, chase reps about pipeline updates. Legitimate, necessary work.

Today, an agent does all of that in minutes. Not hypothetically. I've built these workflows. CRM field updates, activity logging, report generation. Agents handle it without complaining, without forgetting, without taking PTO.

So what's left for RevOps?

The hard stuff. Writing SQL to find patterns the CRM doesn't surface. Building enrichment pipelines that pull signals from 6 sources and score them with custom logic. Designing lead routing that adapts based on real conversion data, not territory maps drawn on a whiteboard.

This isn't a layoff story. It's a skills migration story. The RevOps people who learned to code, who understand data infrastructure, who think in systems rather than spreadsheets. They're becoming the most valuable people on the GTM team.

The ones still manually updating picklist values? That's the work agents eat first.

The gap between these two paths is widening every quarter. And the window to cross over is shrinking.

Builds automated routing logic that goes beyond round-robin. Understands API documentation well enough to connect tools without middleware.

This isn't about replacing people. It's about recognizing that the job description shifted.

When I built my GTM stack, the bottleneck was never "someone to update Salesforce." Agents handle that. The bottleneck was someone who could look at enrichment output, spot where the scoring model was wrong, and rewrite the logic.

That's engineering thinking applied to revenue operations. And it's the profile that's impossible to automate because the value comes from judgment, not execution.

RevOps leaders: update your job descriptions. You're not hiring admins anymore. You're hiring engineers who understand revenue.

posts.title: The feature nobody used
posts.hook: I spent three weeks building a dashboard that exactly zero people opened after launch.
posts.body:
I spent three weeks building a dashboard that exactly zero people opened after launch.

It was beautiful. Real-time charts, filterable by date range, exportable to PDF. Every metric I thought a GTM team would want. Clean code, good tests, responsive design.

Nobody cared.

The thing that actually got used? A Slack bot that posted one number every morning: "You have 7 qualified leads to review." That took an afternoon to build.

The lesson cost me three weeks but saved me from a much worse version of the same mistake on the next project.

What I do differently now:

1. Build the smallest possible version first. Not an MVP. A single output. One number, one alert, one action.
2. See if anyone changes their behavior because of it.
3. Only then add complexity.

The dashboard failed because I was solving for "what data could be useful" instead of "what decision does someone need to make right now."

Every feature I ship now starts with one question: what does the user do differently after seeing this? If I can't answer that in one sentence, I don't build it yet.

remixes.body:
The most used tool in my GTM stack cost me 45 minutes to build.

It's a Slack bot. Every morning at 8am, it posts one message: "You have X qualified leads to review." That's it. No charts. No filters. No export button.

Before the bot, I had a full dashboard. Real-time visualizations, date range filters, PDF exports, responsive layout. Three weeks of development. Beautiful code. Good test coverage.

Usage after launch: zero.

Not low usage. Zero. Nobody opened it. Not once.

Here's what I learned: the dashboard answered questions nobody was asking. People didn't want to explore data. They wanted to know one thing. Do I have leads to work today, yes or no.

The Slack bot met them where they already were, in the tool they check every 30 seconds, with the only number that changed their next action.

I've seen this pattern repeat across every GTM tool I've built since. The thing that gets adopted is never the most complete solution. It's the one that fits into an existing behavior with the least friction.

Now I start every build by asking: what's the one number, and where does the person already look?

remixes.label: anti-dashboard-manifesto
remixes.hook: Dashboards are where data goes to be ignored.
remixes.body:
Dashboards are where data goes to be ignored.

I know because I've built them. Beautiful ones. Filterable, exportable, real-time. Every metric a GTM team could want, arranged in a clean grid with good typography.

Three weeks of work. Zero opens after launch.

The problem isn't the data or the design. The problem is the interaction model. A dashboard says "come find your answer." It requires someone to stop what they're doing, navigate to a different tool, remember what they were looking for, and interpret what they see.

You know what works? Push, don't pull.

A Slack message at 8am: "7 qualified leads to review." That's it. One number. In the tool they're already staring at. Tied directly to an action they need to take.

After that experience, I rebuilt my approach to internal tools entirely. Every output is a push notification, not a pull dashboard. Alerts in Slack. Summaries in email. Scores appended directly to the CRM record.

The best internal tool is the one nobody has to remember to open. It finds you, tells you the one thing that matters, and gets out of the way.

posts.title: Ship fast advice is incomplete
posts.hook: "Ship fast and validate" presumes you have the energy to ship 47 things that fail before finding the one that works.
posts.body:
"Ship fast and validate" presumes you have the energy to ship 47 things that fail before finding the one that works.

As a solo founder, I don't have that energy budget. Neither do most people building alone.

The advice works at a startup with a team, funding, and a support system that absorbs the emotional cost of repeated failure. When you're solo, every failed ship costs more than the code. It costs momentum, confidence, and the willingness to open your laptop tomorrow.

What actually works for me:

Ship slow and validate fast.

Spend time with the problem before writing code. Talk to 5 people. Read the Reddit threads. Check if anyone is already paying for a half-broken version of this. THEN build the smallest possible thing.

I wasted months last year shipping features nobody asked for because I was optimizing for speed instead of signal. The turnaround came when I started spending more time in conversations and less time in my editor.

The founders I know who are actually making money aren't the fastest shippers. They're the ones who talked to enough people to know exactly what to build before they opened their IDE.

Speed without direction is just motion.

Nobody talks about the emotional cost per failed launch when you're building alone.

At a funded startup, a failed experiment is a data point. You learn, you iterate, you ship the next thing. There's a team to absorb the disappointment. A standup where someone says "we'll get the next one." A paycheck that arrives regardless.

When you're solo, a failed launch hits different. You spent your weekend on it. You skipped the thing you wanted to do. You put yourself out there and the market shrugged. And now you have to muster the energy to do it again, with nobody splitting the emotional load.

"Ship fast and validate" assumes an infinite energy budget. It assumes the 47th failed experiment feels the same as the first. It doesn't.

So what actually works solo?

I stopped shipping experiments and started shipping infrastructure. Things that compound whether or not any single use case works. An enrichment pipeline I use for every campaign. A content system that distributes one piece across five platforms. Agent workflows I reuse across clients.

Each build teaches me something AND stays useful. The validation isn't "did this specific thing work." It's "am I more capable than I was last week."

That reframe changed everything for me.

"Ship fast" is advice from people who've never had to do the shipping, the marketing, the support, and the bookkeeping in the same afternoon.

I don't mean it's wrong. I mean it's incomplete in a way that causes real damage to solo builders.

The full version should be: ship fast, but choose what to ship with extreme care, because you don't get 47 at-bats. You get maybe 5 or 6 before burnout makes the decision for you.

Here's how I've adapted.

Before building anything, I spend one day just looking. Reading threads where people describe the pain. Checking if competitors exist and whether they're growing or stalling. Asking myself if this is something I'd pay for, honestly.

That one day of research eliminates maybe 80% of ideas I would have spent a week building. Not because they're bad ideas. Because they're ideas with no clear path to someone caring.

The remaining 20% still might fail. But they fail for interesting reasons, not obvious ones. And interesting failures teach you something you can use next time.

Solo building isn't about shipping volume. It's about shot selection. Every build costs you time, energy, and a piece of optimism you can't get back cheaply. Spend them on the shots most likely to connect.

posts.title: One anchor piece, distributed everywhere
posts.hook: I write one thing per week. It shows up in 5 places.
posts.body:
I write one thing per week. It shows up in 5 places.

The workflow:

1. Build something real during the week (enrichment pipeline, email infrastructure, a new agent workflow)
2. Write the build log as a Substack post on Friday
3. Claude Code extracts a LinkedIn post from the build log
4. Same content becomes 2-3 Reddit comments in relevant threads
5. Key insight becomes an X thread
6. The Substack post is also the blog post on my site

One piece of thinking. Five surfaces. Total writing time: maybe 90 minutes on the original post. The rest is extraction and reformatting, which the agent handles.

The teams publishing 5x/week on LinkedIn with diminishing returns are solving the wrong problem. The constraint isn't volume. It's having something worth saying.

When you build in public, you generate one genuine insight per week just by doing your job. That insight, distributed properly, outperforms a content calendar full of recycled frameworks and repackaged advice.

I track this in a simple SQLite table. Each "anchor piece" gets a row, each distribution gets logged. The data is clear: my best-performing content across all platforms traces back to a real build session, not a brainstorming meeting.

Publish less. Distribute more. Build the thing that gives you something to write about.

One input. Five outputs. Zero creative block.

posts.title: The agent didn't replace the BDR team, it replaced the busywork
posts.hook: Every viral post about replacing a team with AI skips the part where a human still makes every important decision.
posts.body:
Every viral post about replacing a team with AI skips the part where a human still makes every important decision.

I run my entire top-of-funnel through Claude Code agents. Research, enrichment, scoring, draft personalization. It's real and it works.

But I review every email before it sends. I approve every sequence. I read the enrichment output and override the scoring when the signal doesn't match the number.

The agent didn't replace judgment. It replaced the 6 hours of copying data between tabs, googling company info, and formatting spreadsheets that used to happen before the judgment part.

When someone says "I replaced 4 BDRs with an agent," what they usually mean is:

- The research step went from 20 min/contact to 30 seconds
- The personalization draft went from scratch to review-and-edit
- The data entry disappeared entirely
- One person with an agent does the throughput of a team

That's a real efficiency gain. But calling it "replacement" misframes the value. The BDR job wasn't the busywork. The busywork was just blocking them from doing the actual job: understanding prospects and having good conversations.

Agents remove the blockage. The human work gets more important, not less.

Month 1 results: pipeline volume up 3x, cost per meeting down 78%. The uncomfortable truth is that most SDR work was always pattern-matching on data — and agents are just better at it.

remixes.label: human-in-the-loop-reality
remixes.hook: My agents do 90% of the outbound work. I do 100% of the thinking.
remixes.body:
My agents do 90% of the outbound work. I do 100% of the thinking.

Here's what that actually looks like in practice.

Monday morning, the pipeline runs. Claude Code agents research target accounts, pull enrichment data from multiple sources, score leads against my ICP criteria, and draft personalized email sequences.

By 9am, I have a queue of 30 enriched, scored, drafted prospects waiting for review.

Then the human part starts. I read every enrichment summary. I override scores when the signal doesn't match the number. I rewrite openings that sound too polished. I kill entire sequences when the targeting feels off.

This takes about an hour. Out of 30 drafts, maybe 18 survive my review. The rest get dropped or reworked.

The agent saved me 6 hours of manual research and drafting. My review added the judgment that makes the emails actually land. Both parts are essential.

The viral narrative is "I replaced my SDR team with AI." The reality is "I replaced the research and first-draft work with AI, then applied more human judgment than most SDR teams ever get time for."

The agent handles volume. The human handles taste. Remove either one and the whole thing falls apart.

remixes.label: trust-but-verify
remixes.hook: I trust my agents with research. I don't trust them with send.
remixes.body:
I trust my agents with research. I don't trust them with send.

That one boundary is the difference between AI-assisted outbound and AI-generated spam.

My agents handle: account research across multiple data sources, lead enrichment and scoring, ICP matching, draft personalization based on signals, sequence assembly.

I handle: reviewing every enrichment output for accuracy, overriding scores when the data says one thing but experience says another, reading every email draft before it sends, approving every sequence before it activates, catching the subtle things an agent misses. Like when a "VP of Sales" is actually a solo consultant, or when a company's website says one thing but their actual product does something else.

The reason this matters goes beyond quality control. When I review agent output, I learn things about my market that the agent can't surface. Patterns in what the scoring gets wrong. Segments I didn't know existed. Signals that correlate with closed deals that aren't in any database.

The review process isn't overhead. It's the most valuable hour of my day.

Every viral "I automated my entire GTM" post is either lying about the human review layer or sending emails that recipients immediately recognize as AI slop. There's no third option.

The agent didn't replace judgment. It replaced the 6 hours of copying data between tabs, googling company info, and formatting spreadsheets that used to happen before the judgment part.

When someone says "I replaced 4 BDRs with an agent," what they usually mean is:

- The research step went from 20 min/contact to 30 seconds
- The personalization draft went from scratch to review-and-edit
- The data entry disappeared entirely
- One person with an agent does the throughput of a team

That's a real efficiency gain. But calling it "replacement" misframes the value. The BDR job wasn't the busywork. The busywork was just blocking them from doing the actual job: understanding prospects and having good conversations.

Agents remove the blockage. The human work gets more important, not less.
